regulatory_approval_status_if_applicable: DERM is a Class III CE marked AI as a Medical Device (AIaMD), indicating the most rigorous assessment in Europe, typically reserved for critical devices. It also holds a UKCA mark as a Class IIa AI medical device. In 2024, DERM was granted its Class III CE-mark. It is the first legally authorized AI device in the world capable of making independent clinical decisions for skin cancer diagnosis without human review. The device fulfills the provisions of the UK Medical Device Regulation 2002 (as amended), EU Medical Device Regulation 2017/745, and New Zealand Medicines (Database of Medical Devices) Regulations 2003. summary: DERM (Deep Ensemble for the Recognition of Malignancy) by Skin Analytics is a Class III CE marked and UKCA marked Class IIa AI medical device designed to assess dermoscopic images of skin lesions. It functions as an autonomous AI system that screens, triages, and assesses patients with suspected skin cancer, generating a suspected diagnosis and referral recommendation. It aims to increase capacity for dermatology services, reduce unnecessary urgent suspected cancer referrals, and decrease waitlists by safely identifying benign lesions and allowing dermatologists to focus on high-risk cases. DERM has been deployed across the NHS, assessing over 150,000 patients and detecting more than 14,000 cancers, with a Negative Predictive Value of 99.8% for melanoma.

intended_use_and_workflow: DERM is an AI-based skin lesion analysis device intended for use in the screening, triage, and assessment of skin lesions suspicious for skin cancer. It analyzes a dermoscopic image of a skin lesion and returns a suspected diagnosis and, if applicable, a referral recommendation. It is primarily used by healthcare organizations as an automated clinical management tool to screen, triage, or assess patients presenting with one or more lesions concerning skin cancer. Its outputs can be used to issue management instructions (e.g., 'refer', 'discharge', 'monitor') without a second read from a human clinician. Healthcare staff use a smartphone with a dermoscopic lens attachment to take high-quality images of suspicious skin lesions, which are then uploaded to DERM's online platform. For lesions identified as pre-cancerous or cancerous, an NHS dermatologist reviews the case virtually. For patients with black or brown skin, an additional healthcare professional review takes place during an evidence generation period. Patients identified as benign are discharged with written advice.
primary_intended_users: DERM is intended to be used by primary care clinicians/providers (e.g., general practitioners, nurse practitioners) and secondary care clinicians/providers (e.g., dermatologists). These users may utilize DERM's outputs as an automated clinical management tool or to augment other clinical data points for decision-making. Medical photographers and patients may be authorized to capture images for submission, but they are not intended to be users of DERM's outputs.
necessary_knowledge_expertise: Users must follow the instructions for use, including the intended use, indications, and safety information. The Client System must be integrated with DERM according to the DERM API User Manual. Users must capture images using approved dermoscopic Image Capture Hardware (Camera Device connected to a Dermoscope using a Connection Kit). Users should also ensure their computer is free of viruses/malware and compliant with local cybersecurity policies. For information on good image-taking technique, users should refer to the 'Hardware, Image Capture, Exclusions & Consent' manual.
how_to_use: DERM is integrated with a third-party client software system. Users (healthcare professionals, non-medical clinical users, or patients) capture dermoscopic images of skin lesions using approved Image Capture Hardware (a Camera Device connected to a Dermoscope via a Connection Kit). These images are submitted to DERM for AI-based analysis. DERM returns a suspected diagnosis and a referral recommendation. These outputs can trigger automated clinical management activities (e.g., patient referral letters) or augment other clinical data for decision-making. For patients with black or brown skin, an additional healthcare professional review is conducted. The latest version of the Instructions For Use in PDF format can be downloaded from the Skin Analytics website.
targeted_patient_population: DERM is indicated for use on dermoscopic images of cutaneous lesions where there is a suspicion of skin cancer in patients aged 18 years or over, in any body location except where specific exclusions apply. It has primarily been evaluated on patients with Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV, reflecting the prevalence of the disease in the general population. It is used for lesions referred for potential skin cancer, detecting malignant, pre-malignant, or non-cancerous (benign) lesions.

developer_supplied_warnings: Skin Analytics Limited cannot accept financial or other responsibilities resulting from the use of its information, software, or devices. Users must ensure compliance with local laws, rules, and regulations. DERM is to be used only by prescription of a healthcare professional or by a clinical organization’s client system for screening, triage, and assessment of skin lesions suspected of skin cancer. DERM does not provide a definitive diagnosis. When used as part of an automated clinical management system, the DERM classification output may trigger an automated clinical management response via a client system; the content and format of this response are the responsibility of the commissioning clinical organization. When DERM augments other clinical data, its result should be viewed alongside all other clinical information before making a clinical management decision. If DERM is unavailable, clinical users should follow existing clinical practice. DERM should not be used for cases or excluded lesions listed in the 'Contraindications' section (e.g., patients under 18, assessing non-cancer skin conditions, monitoring treatment, staging disease, images other than dermoscopic, images not of the identified patient, open/ulcerated lesions, lesions unable to be entirely imaged, lesions obscured by hair/tattoos/scars, lesions beneath nails/eyes/mucosal surfaces/soles of feet/palms of hands, or previously biopsied lesions). DERM does not screen for lesions not listed in its 'Product Information - Device Inputs and Outputs' section (e.g., rare malignant lesions like Merkel Cell Carcinoma). DERM should be used with caution on Fitzpatrick skin types V-VI. Images submitted must be captured using approved dermoscopic Image Capture Hardware, and good image-taking technique is crucial. Dermoscopic images should not be captured with immersion fluid or contain external objects/markers as these could adversely impact performance. DERM only analyzes the submitted dermoscopic image, so users must ensure it is of the correct lesion of concern. If multiple dermoscopic images are submitted, each is assessed in isolation.
model_limitations: DERM should not be used on: patients under the age of 18; for assessing skin conditions where the concern is not skin cancer (e.g., rashes, eczema, infectious diseases, lupus); for monitoring treatment; for staging of disease; for images other than dermoscopic images of skin lesions; for images of skin lesions from a subject other than the identified patient; on open or ulcerated skin lesions; on skin lesions unable to be entirely imaged within the dermoscopic device used; on skin lesions obscured by hair, tattoos, or scars; on skin lesions beneath nails, in eyes, on mucosal surfaces, or on soles of feet or palms of hands; or on skin lesions which have previously been biopsied. DERM does not provide a definitive diagnosis and does not screen for rare malignant lesions such as Merkel Cell Carcinoma. It should be used with caution on Fitzpatrick skin types V-VI, as it has been primarily evaluated on types I-IV. Images submitted for analysis must be captured using approved dermoscopic Image Capture Hardware and should not be captured with immersion fluid or contain any other external objects or markers within the image (e.g., felt-tip marker, sticker, ruler), as these could adversely impact performance. DERM only analyzes the submitted dermoscopic image and does not incorporate other patient or lesion information (e.g., age, lesion location, change, or non-dermoscopic images) captured by the client system in its assessment. If DERM is unavailable, clinical users should continue patient assessment following existing clinical practice. It is not designed for general dermatology documentation outside of lesion triage or for solo practices not integrated with a larger referral system.

ai_system_facts: DERM (Deep Ensemble for the Recognition of Malignancy) is an AI-powered medical device developed by Skin Analytics that specializes in dermatology solutions to improve skin cancer detection and patient care pathways. It is a Class III CE marked AI as a Medical Device (AIaMD) and UKCA marked Class IIa medical device. DERM is the first legally authorized AI device in the world capable of making independent clinical decisions for skin cancer diagnosis without human review. It is built around a custom teledermatology platform and is designed to triage patients with skin lesions, identifying non-cancerous lesions to allow dermatologists to focus on urgent cases. The system has been trained on a vast real-world dataset accumulated over 12 years and recognizes cancerous lesions (melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma), pre-malignant conditions (actinic keratosis, intraepidermal carcinoma/Bowen's disease), and common benign lookalikes. It has been deployed in 26 NHS sites, assessed over 150,000 patients, and detected more than 14,000 cancers.
model_type: DERM is an autonomous AI system that serves as an AI-based skin lesion analysis device. It functions as an automated clinical management tool for screening, triage, and assessment of skin lesions suspicious for skin cancer. It is capable of making independent clinical decisions and can trigger automated clinical management responses (e.g., 'refer,' 'discharge,' or 'monitor') without a second read from a human clinician. It can also be used to augment other clinical data points to support clinical decision-making.
interaction_with_other_systems: DERM is a standalone software device intended to be integrated with a third-party client software system through which images are transmitted to DERM for analysis and results are displayed. The client system can also enable automated clinical management activities (e.g., patient referral letters) to be triggered by DERM outputs. Only images captured by approved dermoscopic hardware systems (a Camera Device connected to a Dermoscope using a Connection Kit) are permitted for submission. The integration must follow instructions in the DERM API User Manual, and Skin Analytics provides an Onboarding process to support this integration. The client system may capture additional patient or lesion information, but this data is not included in DERM's assessment.
outcomes_and_output: DERM assesses dermoscopic images of skin lesions to provide a suspected diagnosis and referral recommendation. It safely triages patients with non-cancerous lesions away from cancer pathways, allowing dermatologists to focus on high-risk cases. This increases capacity, speeds up diagnosis, and reduces unnecessary urgent suspected cancer referrals. In NHS Primary Care, DERM typically avoids urgent suspected cancer referrals for 40-55% of patients, with 40-55% discharged. In Secondary Care, it has helped avoid up to 95% of NHS face-to-face USCRs by combining DERM with downstream teledermatology reviews, routing patients straight to biopsy. It has a Negative Predictive Value of 99.8% for melanoma, meaning it almost never misses a cancer requiring urgent attention, outperforming dermatologists (98.9%) in face-to-face consultations. Since 2020, DERM has safely discharged thousands of patients across the NHS, contributing to robust NHS dermatology cost savings and helping to reduce wait times and clinician workload.
type_and_value_of_solution_output: The solution output is a suspected diagnosis and a referral recommendation for the skin lesion. The suspected diagnosis classifies lesions as cancerous (malignant, e.g., melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma), pre-cancerous (pre-malignant, e.g., Actinic Keratosis, Intraepidermal Carcinoma/Bowen's disease), or non-cancerous (benign). The referral recommendation can be 'refer,' 'discharge,' or 'monitor'. When deployed as an automated clinical management tool, the classification output may trigger an automated clinical management response via a clinical organization's client system, such as a referral letter.
explanation_for_how_an_output_is_generat: DERM employs artificial intelligence (AI)-based algorithms to analyze a dermoscopic image of a skin lesion. It examines visual characteristics of the lesion and compares them to its vast bank of images of known skin conditions, which includes cancerous lesions, pre-malignant conditions, and common benign lookalikes. Based on this analysis, DERM generates a suspected diagnosis and, if applicable, a referral recommendation.

validation_test_dataset:
Validation and testing are based on multiple datasets and evaluations:
1. An independent analysis of 33,693 real-world lesions, including 835 melanomas.
2. A systematic review and meta-analysis of all studies involving consultant dermatologists up to April 2024.
3. Comprehensive real-world evidence derived from the assessment of more than 70,000 patients across 14 NHS sites (at the time of research).
4. A service evaluation by the University of Exeter focused on safety, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness.
5. An independent report by Edge Health, commissioned by NHSE’s Outpatient Recovery and Transformation Programme (OPRT) team, evaluating AI in skin cancer pathways, with much of the report focusing on DERM's performance as it was the only technology meeting requirements for autonomous pathways.
6. An evaluation by Unity Insights with the University of Surrey, covering 9,649 patients across four NHS sites.
7. An evaluation by Edge Health for the East Midlands Academic Health Science Network at University Hospitals Leicester.
8. Powered prospective studies run in the UK, US, and Italy, using images of skin lesions that represent the target population.

Its Negative Predictive Value (NPV) is 99.8% for melanoma, meaning that for every 1000 patients identified by DERM as not having melanoma, 999 truly do not have it. This performance is stated to be better than a dermatologist's face-to-face assessment, which has an NPV of 98.9%. Since 2020, DERM has safely discharged thousands of patients across the NHS. In NHS Primary Care, DERM typically avoids urgent suspected cancer referrals for 40-55% of patients, with 40-55% discharged. In Secondary Care, it has helped avoid significant percentages of NHS face-to-face urgent suspected cancer referrals. Early evidence suggests automated use of DERM could approximately halve the number of referrals to dermatologists within the urgent skin cancer pathway compared to using teledermatology alone. To date, the system has been deployed in 26 NHS sites, assessed over 150,000 patients, and detected more than 14,000 cancers.
safety_reliability_interpretation: The high accuracy (97%) and Negative Predictive Value (99.8% for melanoma) of DERM indicate its reliability in identifying skin cancers and, crucially, in ruling out melanoma, performing better than face-to-face dermatologist assessments in this specific metric. This enables DERM to safely discharge a significant proportion of patients (40-55% in primary care) with benign lesions, thereby reducing unnecessary urgent suspected cancer referrals and freeing up dermatologist capacity. The system's ability to halve referrals to dermatologists while maintaining patient safety demonstrates its effectiveness in improving patient pathways and reducing waiting times without compromising care quality, allowing specialists to focus on high-risk cases.
safety_reliability_test_type: Safety and reliability have been assessed through various types of evaluations: a market-leading approach to performance monitoring, independent analyses of real-world lesions, systematic reviews and meta-analyses of studies involving consultant dermatologists, service evaluations focusing on safety, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness (e.g., by the University of Exeter), independent reports evaluating AI use in skin cancer pathways (e.g., by Edge Health commissioned by NHSE), and real-world evaluations funded by the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) as part of the AI in Health and Care Award (e.g., by Unity Insights with the University of Surrey, and Edge Health for East Midlands Academic Health Science Network). The Class III CE mark also involves a rigorous assessment of medical technology.
safety_reliability_testing_data_descript: Safety and reliability testing data includes: 1. An independent analysis of 33,693 real-world lesions, including 835 melanomas. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis of all studies involving consultant dermatologists up to April 2024. 3. Real-world evaluation data from 9,649 patients across four NHS sites, collected between February 2022 and April 2023. 4. Comprehensive real-world evidence derived from the assessment of more than 70,000 patients across 14 NHS sites (at the time of research). 5. Data from over 150,000 patients assessed across 26 NHS sites, detecting more than 14,000 cancers. DERM has been tested on images of skin lesions representing the population it may be used on, in powered prospective studies conducted in the UK, US, and Italy. Given disease prevalence, DERM was primarily evaluated on patients with Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV.
safety_reliability_validation_process_an: The validation process involves continuous performance monitoring since December 2023 up to Q1 2025 Post Market Surveillance Reports, with analysis based on an independent analysis of real-world lesions and a systematic review of dermatologist studies. Performance targets are set by a Clinical Advisory Committee of leading UK and international dermatologists and health economics experts. External partners, including the University of Exeter, Edge Health, University of Surrey, Unity Insights, Health Enterprise East, York Health Economics Consortium, Imperial Trust, and the Exeter Test Group, have conducted evaluations focusing on safety, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness. DERM's regulatory approval as a Class III CE marked AI medical device for skin cancer, which is the most rigorous assessment in Europe, serves as a continuous commitment to perform against best-in-class standards. The model's autonomous decision-making capability is justified by its proven ability to safely discharge patients without a dermatologist and its performance matching or exceeding face-to-face dermatologist evaluations.
